blocks.content: So far every class you have built (Car, BankAccount, PaymentProcessor) stood alone. But in real systems, many classes are genuinely variations of a more general idea: a SavingsAccount is a kind of BankAccount, a Dog is a kind of Animal. Inheritance is how you express that relationship directly in code.
1. Introduction & Why It Matters

Inheritance lets one class (the subclass) acquire the fields and methods of another class (the superclass), while adding its own new behavior or changing existing behavior. It models an IS-A relationship: a Dog IS-A Animal, a SavingsAccount IS-A BankAccount.

Without inheritance, every similar class would have to rewrite shared behavior from scratch. If SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount both needed deposit() and withdraw(), and neither could inherit from a common BankAccount, you would maintain two separate, duplicate copies of the exact same logic, and any bug fix would need to happen twice.
2. Real-Life Analogy
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884630960-641382642.png
blocks.alt: Animal as a general base with Dog and Cat each adding their own specific behavior

blocks.content: Every dog and every cat can eat and sleep, that is what makes them animals. But a dog also barks, and a cat also meows, behavior neither one shares with the other. Dog and Cat both build on top of the general "Animal" idea instead of redefining "eating" from zero.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884632933-538516226.png
blocks.alt: Vehicle as a general base with Car and Truck each adding their own specific behavior

blocks.content: A vehicle hierarchy works the same way: every Car and every Truck can start and stop, that is what makes them vehicles. A Car additionally opens a trunk, a Truck additionally loads cargo, specific behavior layered on top of shared, general behavior.
3. Problem It Solves & Definition
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884634825-294692922.png
blocks.alt: Duplicated logic across two classes refactored into one shared base class

blocks.content: Inheritance solves the problem of duplicated logic across closely related classes. Rather than copy-pasting deposit() and withdraw() into both SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount, both can extend one shared BankAccount that defines that logic exactly once.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.content: Inheritance is a mechanism where a new class (the subclass or derived class) acquires the fields and methods of an existing class (the superclass or base class), and may add new members or override existing ones. In simple terms: a subclass gets everything the superclass has, for free, and can build on top of it.
4. Key Terminology

["Superclass (or parent/base class): the more general class being extended.","Subclass (or child/derived class): the more specific class that extends the superclass.","extends keyword: declares that one class inherits from another.","IS-A relationship: the conceptual relationship inheritance models, e.g. \"a Dog IS-A Animal.\"","Method overriding: a subclass providing its own version of a method the superclass already defines.","super keyword: refers to the superclass, used to call its constructor or its version of an overridden method.","Single inheritance: Java allows a class to extend only one superclass directly, unlike some other languages."]
items: Superclass (or parent/base class): the more general class being extended.
Subclass (or child/derived class): the more specific class that extends the superclass.
extends keyword: declares that one class inherits from another.
IS-A relationship: the conceptual relationship inheritance models, e.g. "a Dog IS-A Animal."
Method overriding: a subclass providing its own version of a method the superclass already defines.
super keyword: refers to the superclass, used to call its constructor or its version of an overridden method.
Single inheritance: Java allows a class to extend only one superclass directly, unlike some other languages.

blocks.content: 5. Visual Diagram

blocks.alt: Animal as the superclass with Dog extending it, overriding makeSound and adding fetch

blocks.content: Dog gets name and eat() automatically, with zero extra code, simply by extending Animal. It then overrides makeSound() with its own version, and adds a brand new method, fetch(), that Animal does not have at all.

7. Code Breakdown

["class Dog extends Animal declares that Dog inherits every field and method Animal defines.","super(name); inside Dog’s constructor runs Animal’s constructor first, so the inherited name field gets initialized properly.","eat() is never redefined in Dog, calling dog.eat() runs Animal’s exact implementation, inherited as-is.","makeSound() is redefined in Dog, this is overriding, calling dog.makeSound() runs Dog’s version, not Animal’s.","fetch() exists only on Dog, Animal has no concept of it, and a plain Animal reference could never call it."]
items: class Dog extends Animal declares that Dog inherits every field and method Animal defines.
super(name); inside Dog’s constructor runs Animal’s constructor first, so the inherited name field gets initialized properly.
eat() is never redefined in Dog, calling dog.eat() runs Animal’s exact implementation, inherited as-is.
makeSound() is redefined in Dog, this is overriding, calling dog.makeSound() runs Dog’s version, not Animal’s.
fetch() exists only on Dog, Animal has no concept of it, and a plain Animal reference could never call it.

blocks.alt: Three calls on a Dog object: one inherited, one overridden, one Dog-only

blocks.content: Here is exactly which class’s code actually runs for each call:

{"headers":["Step","Call","What runs"],"rows":[["1","dog.eat()","Animal’s eat(), inherited unchanged, prints \"Rex is eating\""],["2","dog.makeSound()","Dog’s own override, prints \"Rex barks: Woof!\", NOT Animal’s generic version"],["3","dog.fetch()","Dog’s own method, Animal has no equivalent at all"]]}
9. Behind the Scenes (Method Resolution)
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884640435-598272120.png
blocks.alt: The runtime checking the subclass first for an override before falling back to the superclass

blocks.content: When dog.makeSound() is called, the JVM does not simply run Animal’s version because the reference happens to be declared as Animal somewhere. It checks the object’s actual class (Dog) first for a matching method. Since Dog overrides makeSound(), that version runs. Only if a subclass does NOT override a method does the JVM fall back to the superclass’s version, exactly what happens with eat() above.
10. Real-World Use Cases & Industry Examples
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884642488-664398582.png
blocks.alt: Inheritance modeling IS-A relationships across e-commerce, banking, social and gaming domains

blocks.content: ["E-commerce: PhysicalProduct and DigitalProduct both extend a shared Product base, sharing fields like price and name.","Banking: SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount both extend BankAccount, sharing deposit()/withdraw() logic.","Social Media: ImagePost and VideoPost both extend a shared Post base, sharing likes and comments handling.","Gaming: Warrior and Mage both extend a shared Character base, sharing health and movement, while each adds its own special ability."]
items: E-commerce: PhysicalProduct and DigitalProduct both extend a shared Product base, sharing fields like price and name.
Banking: SavingsAccount and CurrentAccount both extend BankAccount, sharing deposit()/withdraw() logic.
Social Media: ImagePost and VideoPost both extend a shared Post base, sharing likes and comments handling.
Gaming: Warrior and Mage both extend a shared Character base, sharing health and movement, while each adds its own special ability.

blocks.content: Some of the most widely used class hierarchies in Java itself follow this exact same pattern:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1784884644573-797453641.png
blocks.alt: Java’s exception hierarchy: Throwable at the root, branching into Exception and its own subclasses

blocks.content: Java’s own exception system is a real inheritance hierarchy: Throwable is the root, Exception extends it, and specific exceptions like IOException and RuntimeException extend Exception further, each layer adding more specific meaning while inheriting the general "this is a throwable problem" behavior.
11. Advantages & Limitations

{"headers":["Advantages","Limitations"],"rows":[["Shared logic is written once in the superclass and reused by every subclass.","Deep inheritance chains (five or six levels) become hard to trace and reason about."],["Subclasses can be used anywhere the superclass is expected, thanks to the IS-A relationship.","Changing the superclass can unintentionally break every subclass that depends on it."],["Overriding lets a subclass customize just the behavior that genuinely needs to differ.","Java allows only single inheritance of classes, forcing some designs toward interfaces instead."]]}
12. Common Mistakes & Best Practices
12.1 Common Mistakes

["Using inheritance for convenience even when the relationship is not truly IS-A, e.g. making Stack extend Vector just to reuse its methods.","Forgetting to call super(...) explicitly when the superclass constructor needs arguments, causing a compile error.","Overriding a method but forgetting the @Override annotation, silently creating a brand new method instead of actually overriding, if the signature does not match exactly.","Building deep hierarchies \"just in case,\" when a shallow hierarchy or composition would model the problem more clearly."]
items: Using inheritance for convenience even when the relationship is not truly IS-A, e.g. making Stack extend Vector just to reuse its methods.
Forgetting to call super(...) explicitly when the superclass constructor needs arguments, causing a compile error.
Overriding a method but forgetting the @Override annotation, silently creating a brand new method instead of actually overriding, if the signature does not match exactly.
Building deep hierarchies "just in case," when a shallow hierarchy or composition would model the problem more clearly.

blocks.content: 12.2 Best Practices

["Only use inheritance when the IS-A relationship is genuinely true, \"a Dog IS-A Animal\" holds up, \"a Stack IS-A Vector\" does not really.","Always add @Override on intentionally overridden methods, so the compiler catches signature mistakes immediately.","Keep shared logic in the superclass minimal and stable, so changes to it are less likely to ripple unexpectedly into subclasses.","Prefer composition over inheritance when you just need to reuse behavior without a true IS-A relationship."]
items: Only use inheritance when the IS-A relationship is genuinely true, "a Dog IS-A Animal" holds up, "a Stack IS-A Vector" does not really.
Always add @Override on intentionally overridden methods, so the compiler catches signature mistakes immediately.
Keep shared logic in the superclass minimal and stable, so changes to it are less likely to ripple unexpectedly into subclasses.
Prefer composition over inheritance when you just need to reuse behavior without a true IS-A relationship.

blocks.content: 13. Key Takeaways & Cheat Sheet

["Inheritance lets a subclass acquire a superclass’s fields and methods, modeling a genuine IS-A relationship.","A subclass can use inherited methods unchanged, override them with its own version, or add entirely new methods.","super(...) calls the superclass constructor, and must run before the rest of the subclass constructor’s own logic.","Method resolution always checks the object’s actual class first, falling back to the superclass only if no override exists.","Inheritance is powerful but easy to overuse, reach for it only when IS-A genuinely holds, not just for code reuse."]
items: Inheritance lets a subclass acquire a superclass’s fields and methods, modeling a genuine IS-A relationship.
A subclass can use inherited methods unchanged, override them with its own version, or add entirely new methods.
super(...) calls the superclass constructor, and must run before the rest of the subclass constructor’s own logic.
Method resolution always checks the object’s actual class first, falling back to the superclass only if no override exists.
Inheritance is powerful but easy to overuse, reach for it only when IS-A genuinely holds, not just for code reuse.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.content: If asked "when should you NOT use inheritance," the fastest correct answer is: when the relationship is not a genuine IS-A, or when you only want to reuse some behavior without wanting the subclass to be substitutable everywhere the superclass is expected, in that case, composition is usually the better tool.
